sn14.11:1.4: This set of seven offers a unique perspective on familiar meditations.
sn14.11:3.1: Whereas “luminosity” (_ābhā_) is often the radiance of the sun and moon in the darkness of space ([mn123:7.4]()), or the light cast by a flame ([mn43:22.18]()), here it is the illumination that appears in deep meditation. Just as in the visual sense, light only manifests in contrast with darkness, in meditation the appearance of luminous radiance is a mode of perception by which the mind communicates to itself the ending of the hindrances and the arising of unclouded awareness. This is why this light came to be called a “sign” (_nimitta_).
sn14.11:3.2: “Beauty” (_subha_) is the focus of wholly pure and exalted meditations, such as the meditation on love, or the sight of a pure brilliant color like the sky ([mn77:22.6]()). It contrasts with the meditation on “ugliness”, such as the parts of the body or a decomposing corpse. At [an6.41:2.7](), Sāriputta explains that an accomplished meditator could see a tree as nothing but beauty or nothing but ugliness, since both of those elements are present in it.
sn14.11:3.3: It is only possible to develop the formless attainments based on the prior development of “form” absorptions, which ultimately have a material basis in the body of the meditator and in the meditation subject such as the breath, or the luminous “form” that arises as a guide into absorption.
